l: rape of Helen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The rape of Helen is the abduction of Helen by Paris from her husband, Menelaüs. It causes the Greeks to unite their forces and undertake the expedition against Troy.

l: sacrifice of Iphigenia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The sacrifice of Iphigenia is demanded by Calchas as the means of appeasing Diana and obtaining favorable winds. Iphigenia is led to the altar, but Diana substitutes a hind, so the maiden is not sacrificed.

l: Calchas's prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Calchas's prophecy interprets a serpent devouring eight birds, foretells Greek conquest and Troy's fall, assigns the war nine years, and requires a virgin's sacrifice for success.

l: serpent-and-birds omen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: occurs_at Aulis [during a sacrifice to Jupiter] The serpent-and-birds omen occurs at Aulis during a Greek sacrifice to Jupiter. An azure serpent devours eight birds and their mother, and Calchas interprets the event as predicting victory after nine years of war.

l: landing of the Greeks at Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The landing of the Greeks at Troy is opposed by the Trojans, who defend the shore. Protesilaüs is the first Greek to die, and fighting begins between the two forces.

l: death of Protesilaüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The death of Protesilaüs occurs when he is the first Greek to land on the Trojan shore and is killed by Hector. His death is presented as decreed by fate.

l: duel of Achilles and Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: ends_in transformation of Cygnus [after Achilles defeats Cygnus] The duel of Achilles and Cygnus begins when Achilles singles out Cygnus after Cygnus has killed many Greeks. Achilles's weapons cannot wound Cygnus, but Achilles eventually throws him down and chokes him with the straps of his helmet.

l: transformation of Cygnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The transformation of Cygnus occurs after Achilles defeats him. Neptune changes his body into a white swan, leaving his armor behind.

l: Grecian chiefs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Grecian chiefs assemble at a truce-time feast after Achilles’s victory over Cygnus, discuss Cygnus and hear Nestor’s account of Cæneus, then sit in judgment over Ajax and Ulysses’ contest and award Achilles’ armour to Ulysses.

l: feast, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a festive meal [attended by the chiefs] A feast follows the truce between the Greeks and the Trojans, with the chiefs eating roasted flesh and drinking wine while discussing valor. The wedding feast of Pirithoüs and Hippodame later becomes the scene of violence when Eurytus attacks the bride.

l: Cænis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cænis, Elatus’s beautiful Thessalian daughter, is desired by many suitors and assaulted by Neptune on a lonely shore; afterward, she asks Neptune to make her no longer a woman and protect her from such violence.

l: Hippodame, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_married_to Pirithoüs [as his bride] Hippodame is the bride of Pirithoüs and is praised for her beauty at the wedding feast. Eurytus seizes her by the hair, causing the conflict between the Centaurs and Lapithæ.

l: Battle of the Centaurs and Lapithæ, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Battle of the Centaurs and Lapithæ is a battle arising at Pirithoüs’s wedding feast. It begins when Eurytus and other Centaurs attack Hippodame and other women. Centaurs and Lapiths fight with banquet objects, weapons, trees, and stones; many are killed, and Cæneus is buried beneath trees. By night the surviving Centaurs flee or disperse, retreating to Arcadia as pursuing Lapithæ drive them toward Malea.

l: Cæneus's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cæneus’s transformation is Cænis’s change from woman to man. After asking Neptune to prevent another similar assault, Cænis is granted the request; the voice becomes hoarser and seemingly male. Later, Cæneus appears as an unwoundable male warrior, though Latreus calls his male resemblance false.

l: Cæneus's death and transformation into a bird, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cæneus's death and transformation occur when the Centaurs, unable to wound him with weapons, bury him beneath piled tree trunks. The weight covers his face and head and deprives him of air, pressing him to death. Afterward, Neptune changes his body into a tawny-winged bird seen emerging from the pile.

l: invulnerability, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cygnus and Cæneus are presented as men whose bodies cannot be pierced or wounded by weapons. Cygnus’s invulnerability amazes the Grecian chiefs, while the Centaurs overcome Cæneus only by crushing him beneath tree trunks.

l: Thessalians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Thessalians, some living near Mount Pelion, train and use horses instead of chariots, perfect horsemanship, excel among Greeks, and become associated with horsemen and bull-killing Hippocentaurs or Centaurs.

l: horsemanship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Horsemanship was said to have been perfected by the Thessalians, although one account considers the Lapithæ’s claim to have perfected it more probable. The discussion also suggests that Centaurs may have represented rude, horse-riding mountain tribes.

l: Hippocentaurs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippocentaurs are Thessalians, named for skilled horsemanship and hunting and killing wild bulls.

l: Hippodamia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippodamia, bride of Pirithoüs, was targeted by Eurytus or Eurytion at her wedding, provoking the Centaur-Lapith conflict; one interpretation calls her a Centauress.

l: Hippodamia's wedding, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_attended_by Centaurs [because Hippodamia was supposedly a Centauress] At Hippodamia’s wedding to Pirithoüs, Eurytus, or Eurytion, attempted to seize the bride. This incident led to the battle between the Centaurs and the Lapithæ.

l: war between the Centaurs and Pirithoüs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_resolved friendly_terms [after the quarrel was made up] The Centaurs declared war against Pirithoüs because they claimed, as descendants of Ixion, a right to share in the succession to his dominions. The quarrel was later reconciled, but renewed hostility followed the attempt on Hippodamia.

l: attempt on Hippodamia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_committed_by Eurytus [also called Eurytion] Eurytus, or Eurytion, attempted to seize Hippodamia, the bride of Pirithoüs. The attempt caused the consequences associated with the battle between the Centaurs and the Lapithæ.

l: Italy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Italy is the land to which Hercules directs Myscelos. Myscelos sails there across the Ionian sea and establishes a city on its shores.

l: Periclymenus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Periclymenus, son of Neleus and brother of Nestor, receives from Neptune the power to change shape. During combat with Hercules, he becomes an eagle; Hercules shoots him with an arrow, which enters his neck and kills him.

l: eagle (Periclymenus), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Periclymenus assumes the form of an eagle, using its wings, curved bill, and hooked talons to tear Hercules's face. Hercules wounds it in the joint between the wing and side, causing it to fall and die.

l: arrow (Apollo's), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Apollo directs Paris's unerring arrow toward Achilles with a fatal right hand. The arrow mortally wounds Achilles in the heel, described as the only vulnerable part of his body.

l: the arms of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The arms of Achilles are made by Vulcan at Thetis’s request and belong to Achilles during his life. After Achilles dies, they become the prize in a dispute between Ajax, son of Telamon, and Ulysses. Ajax cites kinship and battlefield service; Ulysses cites discovering Achilles, carrying his body and arms, and aiding Troy’s conquest. Agamemnon leaves the decision to Argive leaders, who award the arms to Ulysses.

l: death of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Achilles's death occurs when Apollo directs Paris's arrow into his vulnerable heel; his body is burned with little ash remaining, while his enduring glory is said to fill the whole world.

l: the contest for Achilles’ arms, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: After Achilles dies, his arms become the subject of a dispute between Ajax and Ulysses. Agamemnon transfers judgment to the assembled Argive leaders. Before the Greek chiefs, Ajax argues from lineage, courage, and service and attacks Ulysses’ speech and stratagem, while Ulysses argues his claim. The chiefs award Achilles’ arms to Ulysses, who wins through his speech.

l: Polyxena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Priam's royal, captive, chaste daughter is led from Hecuba to Achilles' tomb, courageously sacrificed by Neoptolemus, and asks her unburned body be returned to her mother.

l: Pelasgians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: are besiegers of Troy The Greeks witness Ajax’s deeds and are addressed by him during the contest. They had prayed that Ajax would face Hector, and they previously left Philoctetes on Lemnos and accepted Ulysses’ accusations against Palamedes.

l: Grecian fleet, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Grecian fleet, a thousand ships, is threatened by Trojans and Jupiter; Ajax defends it against fire and attack.

l: seven-fold shield of Ajax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ajax is identified as the lord of the seven-fold shield. He says that his shield protected Diomedes and that he used it to defend the Grecian fleet.

l: arrows of Hercules, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: are_possessed_by Philoctetes The arrows of Hercules are possessed by Philoctetes. Although Philoctetes is suffering on Lemnos, he uses the arrows to shoot birds; they are later brought to the siege of Troy and help accomplish Troy’s destined destruction.

l: Ajax’s suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_caused_by the loss of the contest for Achilles’ arms [after Ulysses receives the arms] After Ulysses receives Achilles’ arms, Ajax is overcome by anger and grief. He declares that his sword is still his own, plunges it into his breast, and dies; his blood causes a purple flower to grow from the earth.

l: capture and sack of Troy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: causes death of Priam and] The fall of Troy involved the destruction of Ilion, the death of Priam, the enslavement of the Dardanian matrons, and the burning of the city’s roofs and temples. Astyanax was thrown from the towers, and Hecuba was carried away after mourning the dead.

l: the statue of Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Palladium is a hidden statue of Minerva believed to guard Troy’s safety and required by the Fates for Troy’s capture. During the night Ulysses takes it from Troy, later reveals it before the chiefs as his final appeal, and sails away; some writers link its possession to his dispute with Ajax Telamon.

l: Ulysses’ speech, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ulysses’ speech presents him as the chief source of Greek victories through intelligence, eloquence, and daring rather than physical strength alone. Its eloquence moves the chiefs, who award him the arms of Achilles.

l: Polydorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Polydorus, youngest surviving male child of Priam and Hecuba, is entrusted to Polymnestor for secret private upbringing and protected by Ilione, who raises him as her son. After Phrygian fortunes are ruined, Polymnestor murders him with Thracian weapons and throws his body into the waters; Hecuba finds his wounded corpse on the shore.

l: Polymnestor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Polymnestor is a king of Thrace, ruling Bistonia and described as an Odrysian king, greedy and treacherous. He keeps Polydorus in his rich palace to be raised, but after Phrygian fortunes fail, murders his fosterchild for entrusted riches and casts the body into water. Lured by Hecuba’s promise of treasure, he is attacked by Hecuba and captive Trojan matrons, who tear out his eyes.

l: Palladium dispute, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_between Ulysses and Ajax Telamon [according to Dictys, Suidas, and Cedrenus] and] According to Dictys, Suidas, and Cedrenus, Ajax Telamon and Ulysses disputed possession of the Palladium, and the Grecian nobles awarded it to Ulysses. Other accounts instead make the dispute concern the armour of Achilles.

l: story of Polydorus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: and] The story of Polydorus concerns his being sent by Priam to Polymnestor for secret upbringing, followed by his murder when the fortunes of the Phrygians collapsed. The explanation adds that, in another version, Ilione secretly raised Polydorus as her own son, Polymnestor accidentally killed his own son Deiphylus, and Polydorus later learned the truth and deprived Polymnestor of sight.

l: Memnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Memnon, son of Tithonus and Aurora and a warrior allied with Troy, fights for his uncle on the Phrygian plains, is slain by Achilles, and is honoured through a funeral whose pyre creates the Memnonides.

l: Memnonides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Memnonides are a flock of birds born from Memnon's funeral pyre; each year, after the Sun passes through twelve signs, they divide into opposing groups and perish fighting in honor of their parent.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_for Achilles [to appease his ghost] The sacrifice of Polyxena is demanded by Achilles' ghost as an offering for his tomb. Neoptolemus performs it, and Polyxena dies while asking that her body be returned to Hecuba.

l: Hecuba's transformation into a bitch, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: occurs_in Thrace [near the Sithonian plains] Hecuba's transformation into a bitch follows her revenge against Polymnestor and the attack by the Thracian people. Her mouth becomes suited to barking, and she howls through the Sithonian plains.

l: funeral of Memnon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: produces Memnonides [from its ashes] The funeral of Memnon includes a lofty pyre whose fires sink after Jupiter grants Aurora's request. Its smoke, embers, and ashes gather into living birds that become the Memnonides.

l: tomb of Achilles, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: receives sacrifice of Polyxena [as an offering to Achilles' shade] The tomb of Achilles is the place where Polyxena is sacrificed to appease his ghost. Hecuba says that Achilles remains an enemy of her family even from his tomb.

l: Achilles' ghost, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: requests sacrifice of Polyxena [to honour Achilles' tomb and appease his ghost] Achilles' ghost rises before the Greeks and reproaches them for leaving without remembering his valor. It demands that Polyxena be slain so that his sepulchre will not lack honor.

l: Hecuba's revenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hecuba's revenge begins after Polymnestor murders Polydorus; she lures him with a false treasure promise, then captive matrons help tear out his eyes.

l: Æneas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æneas is a Trojan and Cytherean hero, son of Anchises and Venus, father of Ascanius and Iulus, and foster child of Caieta. After Troy is taken, he escapes its ruins carrying Anchises and the Penates, travelling by sea with Ascanius and companions toward Italy. At Delos, Anius receives him; he consults Apollo’s oracle, exchanges gifts, and receives a goblet. Winds bring him to the Libyan coast and Dido, but he leaves, returns to Eryx and Acestes, and honors Anchises’s tomb with sacrifice. Seeking his father’s shade, he enters the regions of the dead under the Sibyl’s guidance, sees Anchises and ancestors, and learns of future wars. He rescues Achæmenides, reaches Latium, and gains Latinus’s house and daughter through marriage alliance, though warfare follows. His arms prevail; Venus purifies and transforms him into Indiges. Through his descendants, Troy gains a new city, Rome, and Iulus’s power becomes established.

l: Ascanius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ascanius, also called Iulus, son of Æneas, escapes Troy with Æneas and Anchises, travels to Delos, receives parting gifts from Anius, and rules Alba and the Latin state.

l: Anius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Anius, king of Delos and priest of Apollo, receives Æneas, Anchises, and Ascanius, recounts his daughters’ fate, consults Apollo’s oracle, and sends the departing Trojans away with gifts.

l: Anius’s daughters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Anius’s four daughters receive extraordinary gifts from Liber, transforming things by touch into corn, wine, and Minerva’s oil. Compelled by the son of Atreus to provision the Argive fleet, they seek Bacchus’s help and end as snow-white doves.

l: doves of Cytherea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a birds [snow-white and consecrated to Venus] Doves are the bird forms assumed by Anius’s daughters after Bacchus answered their plea for help. They are described as the birds sacred to Venus, whom the text identifies as Anchises’s consort.

l: daughters of Orion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orion’s daughters are sacrificial victims who offer themselves, are carried and burned to end Thebes’s plague; afterward, twin youths arise from their ashes.

l: Coronae, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Coronae is the name Fame gives to twin youths arising from the daughters of Orion’s ashes; they lead their mothers’ funeral procession.

l: Ambracia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ambracia is a city in Epirus, beheld by Æneas and his companions; Apollo, Diana, and Hercules contest it, and its judge becomes stone after favoring Hercules.

l: Dodona, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: contains Dodonaean oracle [in its forest] Dodona is a land whose oaks are described as vocal, and it is associated with an oracle. The account says that traditions variously connected its responses with oaks, beeches, pigeons, or ringing cauldrons.

l: Dodonaean oracle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Dodonaean oracle, famous for ambiguous, ingenious responses, originated with three priestesses and later two priests; accounts describe Selli, sacred trees, pigeons, and wind-struck cauldrons.

l: Polyphemus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Polyphemus is a one-eyed Cyclops, Neptune’s son, a Sicilian shepherd with a mountain cave and many herds. He loves Galatea, changes himself to please her, and boasts of his wealth and strength. Jealous when she loves Acis, he kills Acis with a mountain fragment. After devouring Ulysses’ companions and being blinded by Ulysses, he rages around Ætna, hurling rocks and threatening the escaping Greeks.

l: Acis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Acis, a Sicilian youth, son of Faunus and Symæthis, mutually loves Galatea. Discovered with her by Polyphemus, he flees and calls for help, but is crushed by a mountain fragment and becomes the Acis River.

l: Galatea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Galatea, daughter of Nereus and Doris, is a sea Nymph protected by the Nereids. She loves Acis and rejects Polyphemus; after Polyphemus kills Acis, she changes his blood and remains into a river.

l: the Cyclops, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Cyclops are a huge, lawless pastoral race in Sicily, living in mountain caves from spontaneous produce and flocks. They have one central forehead eye, are associated with Vulcan as workmen, and include the fierce, violent Polyphemus.

l: Scylla, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Scylla is a maiden and sea nymph who lives near the sea. She flees and rejects Glaucus despite his desire and pleas. Circe transforms her into a monster, whom Scylla hates; Scylla then deprives Ulysses of his companions in revenge before becoming Scylla rock.

l: the Acis River, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Sicilian river named Acis arises where Acis is crushed, flowing blood-red before becoming clear while retaining Acis's ancient name.

l: Acis's transformation into a river, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Acis’s transformation into a river is the only change allowed by the Fates after his death: crushed, he becomes a stream, and emerges as a larger river youth with reeds around his horns.

l: Glaucus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Glaucus is a mortal fisherman, later a sea God, associated with Anthedon. He discovers grass that revives fish; after eating it, strange passions drive him into the sea, where he is transformed and then purified by Oceanus and Tethys. He has a green beard and finny tail. Loving Scylla, he seeks Circe’s help after Scylla rejects him, but rejects Circe’s advances, remains devoted to Scylla, mourns her transformation, and flees alliance with Circe. Accounts also variously name his father, say he drowned, make him Triton, and portray him as appearing to the Argonauts, foretelling Jason, interpreting Nereus, and teaching Apollo prediction.

l: Circe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Circe is a goddess, daughter of Titan and the Sun, who rules an island and inhabits halls in Italy. Skilled in herbs, poisons, enchantments, spells, and an enchanted wand, she uses magic chiefly when desire is rejected. After Glaucus refuses her advances, she transforms Scylla with herbs and incantations; she later drugs Ulysses’ companions and turns them into swine, but restores them when Ulysses resists and compels her. She loves Picus, separates him from his companions, transforms him into a woodpecker when he refuses her, and changes his attendants into wild beasts. Ulysses remains with her for a year.

l: Anthedon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Anthedon, near Eubœa across Euripus, is Glaucus’s native city, where he was transformed, worshipped as a sea God, and remembered through Glaucus’ Leap.

l: magic grass, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Grass revives fish that touch it; after Glaucus eats it, his entrails throb, another nature overtakes his mind, and he enters the sea.

l: transformation of Glaucus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Glaucus changes from a mortal fisherman into a sea God after consuming the grass and undergoing purification by Oceanus and Tethys. He develops a green beard, flowing hair, large shoulders, azure arms, and legs that taper into a fish's fin, along with a changed mind.

l: Dido, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Dido, a Sidonian and Belus’s daughter, married Sicharbas, founded Carthage, received Æneas with affection, and killed herself after he abandoned her.

l: Pithecusæ, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pithecusæ are barren, hill-situated islands encountered by Æneas’s ship, named after the Cercopes because of their ape transformation.

l: Scylla rock, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a rock [prominent with crags and avoided by sailors] The rock is what Scylla becomes before she can overwhelm the Trojan ships. It remains prominent with crags and is avoided by sailors.

l: Scylla’s bathing bay, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Scylla’s bathing bay is a small, bow-curved retreat from sea and weather; at highest sun, Circe pollutes it with drugs before Scylla enters.

l: Scylla’s monster transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Scylla’s transformation, caused by Circe’s herbs and poisons, begins while bathing as barking monsters replace her lower body with Cerberean jaws and savage bodies.

l: Dido’s suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Dido’s suicide follows Æneas’s abandonment: she falls on his sword with a poniard atop a funeral pile disguised as sacred rites.

l: Jupiter’s transformation of the Cercopes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: transforms the Cercopes [into apes or ugly animals] Jupiter transforms the Cercopes so that they appear unlike men while still resembling them. He changes their bodies, covers them with long yellow hair, removes their ordinary speech, and leaves them able only to complain with harsh jabbering.

l: burning of the Trojan fleet, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Turnus carries torches against Aeneas’s pine-built ships, and the flames burn the pitch, wax, masts, sails, and benches. Cybele intervenes before the fleet is destroyed.

l: the poisoned fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a polluted bathing place [infected by Circe] The text describes a little bay rather than a fountain as the place Circe poisons. She sprinkles it with juices from a noxious root and uses it to bring about Scylla’s monstrous transformation.

l: Circe’s herbs and poisons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a poisonous magical substance [used against Scylla] Circe bruises herbs infamous for their horrid juices and mixes them with incantations of Hecate. She uses their poisonous power to infect Scylla’s bathing place and transform Scylla.

l: Scylla’s dogs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: are_a Cerberean jaws [occupying Scylla’s lower limbs] Scylla’s dogs emerge from her body as barking monsters. She tries to drive them away, but they remain attached to her and become the jaws and savage forms that make up her transformed body.

l: Circe’s sorcery, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Circe’s sorcery combines potent herbs, noxious juices, and spoken incantations. She mutters a mysterious charm over the polluted bay and uses this magic to change Scylla into a monster. Circe’s magic combines secret drugs, a wand, and spoken charms to transform men into swine. Her magic is reversed through different plants, a blow from her inverted wand, and counter-charms, which restore the companions’ human bodies.

l: Sibyl, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Sibyl is a prophetess of extraordinary longevity who, after rejecting Apollo’s offers, remains unmarried. She guides Aeneas through Avernus to visit Anchises and explains that Apollo granted long life without lasting youth; as vigor fades, she endures crazy old age, retaining only her prophetic voice.

l: Eubœan city, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a region [abounding in the sedge of the swamp and containing the Sibyl’s cavern] Cumæ is described as a region containing marsh sedge and the cavern of the long-lived Sibyl. The Cumæan Sibyl is associated with this place.

l: Avernus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a underworld region [containing the woods of Juno of Avernus] Avernus is the realm through which Aeneas travels to visit the shade of Anchises. Its Juno is identified as Proserpine, and its woods contain the golden branch that the Sibyl directs Aeneas to pluck.

l: Sibylline verses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Sibylline verses, attributed to the Sibyls, were used by early Christian writers to support Christianity; surviving verses openly contain Christian mysteries, Jesus Christ, and the Virgin Mary, so are now generally considered spurious or heavily interpolated.

l: Christianity, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_supported_by Sibylline verses [according to early Christian writers] Early fathers of the church, the Emperor Constantine, and St. Augustin used alleged Sibylline predictions to support the truths of Christianity. The explanation says that the surviving Sibylline verses are generally considered spurious or largely fictitious.

l: Numa Pompilius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa Pompilius is a Roman king, destined by Fame for sovereignty and later voluntarily invited to rule the Roman people. Seeking knowledge, he investigates the nature of things, travels to a city associated with Hercules, asks about its Grecian founder, and is drawn by Pythagoras’s reputation to hear his discourses. Knowing Sabine ceremonials, with Egeria as wife and the Muses as guides, he teaches sacrificial rites and arts of peace to people accustomed to savage warfare. He consults Egeria in the Arician grove about laws, and is said to use divine communications, secret interviews, consultations with the Muses, and hydromancy to confirm belief in communication with heaven and secure obedience. Some accounts call this a political fiction. Romans consider his governing inspired; his reign is marked by profound peace, piety, justice, and civilization. After a long life and completed reign, he dies, mourned by matrons, people, and Senators.

l: Sibyls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Sibyls are women of antiquity who, in frenzied enthusiasm, utter obscure prophetic sentences. Ancient writers variously counted one to ten, naming several regional Sibyls; Plato and others regarded them as benefactors of mankind.

l: Roman Sibylline books, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Roman Sibylline books were a collection of verses attributed to the Sibyls, kept beneath the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus and consulted during public calamities, including pestilence; they directed bringing Æsculapius from Epidaurus to Rome. Guarded by successive officials and repeatedly revised, the original burned with the Capitol, and the remaining books were ultimately burned.

l: Achæmenides, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Achæmenides, an Ithacan Greek, is deserted near Ætna after Polyphemus, survives hidden on wild food, then is rescued by a Trojan ship; he praises Æneas and recounts Polyphemus’ terrifying cannibalistic rage.

l: leather bag of winds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_made_of leather Æolus gives Ulysses a leather bag containing the winds as a gift. When Ulysses’ sailors open it out of envy and a desire for booty, the winds escape and cause the ship to lose its progress.

l: island of Circe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ulysses’ company fastens its ships to the shores of Circe’s island after reaching it. Macareus warns Æneas to avoid the shores of Circe.

l: moly, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a white flower [with a black root] The Cyllenian peace-bearer gives Ulysses a white flower called moly, which has a black root. Protected by it and instructed by the gods, Ulysses resists Circe’s treacherous potion.

l: transformation of Ulysses' companions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: A transformation into swine caused by Circe’s drugged mixture and wand; Ulysses intervenes, and Circe reverses it with harmless plants, an inverted wand, and counter-charms, restoring human forms.

l: Picus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Picus is a young, handsome king of Ausonia, son of Saturn, devoted to horses, hunting, augury, and his wife Canens. Carrying javelins and wearing a purple, gold-fastened cloak, he rejects Circe despite other Nymphs' desire. Circe transforms him into a woodpecker, his clothing becoming plumage; after death he is ranked among Latium's Dii Indigetes.

l: Canens, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Canens is a Nymph, daughter of Janus and Venilia, famed for beauty and extraordinarily powerful singing. Faithful to Picus, she searches six days and nights after his disappearance, then grieves beside the Tiber until she dissolves into light air and sound.

l: Tiber, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: surrounds Island of the Tiber [by its channel] The Tiber surrounds the island that becomes Æsculapius’s Roman dwelling. Its mouths are reached by the ship carrying the god, and its flowing water divides around the Island of the Tiber.

l: Aricia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Aricia contains the thick groves and lake where Egeria hid after Numa's death. Her mourning there disturbed the sacred rites of Diana.

l: Canens (place), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_named_after Canens [the Nymph] The place where Canens disappears is afterward called Canens, preserving the name of the Nymph.

l: the woodpecker, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Picus, transformed by Circe into a woodpecker, retains purple wings and golden neck, strikes wild oak branches, and is tamed for Picus's augury.

l: the transformation of Picus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Circe, rejected by Picus, touches him with her wand and charms, transforming him into a winged woodpecker of Latian woods retaining only his name.

l: Canens's disappearance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Canens, grieving after searching for Picus beside the Tiber, melts away into light air; her disappearance gives its name to the place Canens.

l: Circe's enchantment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Circe creates a phantom boar to lure Picus away from his horse and guards, darkens the sky, summons strange gods and Hecate, and causes supernatural signs to appear. She then touches Picus's attendants with her wand, transforming each of them into a different wild beast.

l: Turnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Turnus, a Rutulian once betrothed to Lavinia, angrily wages war against Aeneas over her, burns Aeneas’s ships, persists despite the fleet’s transformation, and is killed after Aeneas’s victory.

l: Lavinia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Lavinia is the daughter of Latinus and the woman betrothed to Turnus. Latinus gives her to Aeneas in accordance with the oracle concerning a foreign prince.

l: Quirinus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Quirinus is the god and deified form of Romulus, united with Ora and associated with the Roman king’s hill, grove, and temple.

l: Ardea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ardea, Turnus's capital while he lives, falls after his death, burns, and from its ashes rises a bird retaining its name and traits.

l: Rutulians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Rutulians continue the war after Diomedes refuses to send aid. They persist even after Aeneas’s fleet is transformed, while their side is supported by its own deities.

l: war between Aeneas and Turnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The war begins because Latinus gives Lavinia to Aeneas even though she had been promised to Turnus. Etruria and Latium fight with foreign allies, and the conflict continues until Turnus falls.

l: Diomedes's companions' transformation into birds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a divine punishment [inflicted by Venus] After Agmon provokes Venus, his voice, body, arms, feet, and mouth become birdlike. Lycus, Idas, Nycteus, Rhetenor, and Abas undergo the same transformation, and most of Diomedes’s remaining companions fly away as birds resembling white swans.

l: Apulian shepherd's transformation into a wild olive tree, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: results_in wild olive tree [after insulting the Nymphs] An Apulian shepherd frightens and then insults the Nymphs while mimicking their dances. Before a tree closes his throat, he continues speaking, and he is transformed into a wild olive tree whose bitter berries represent the infamy and coarseness of his speech.

l: transformation of Aeneas's ships into sea nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_caused_by Cybele [to preserve the ships from fire] Cybele cuts the fleet’s cables and causes the ships to sink beneath the ocean, where their wood changes into flesh. Their sterns, oars, keel, cordage, and yards become parts of sea Nymphs, who aid ships in danger unless they carry Greeks.

l: death of Turnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Turnus falls after the warfare between his forces and Aeneas’s side. His fall occurs before Ardea is consumed by fire.

l: burning of Ardea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: produces birds [a bird arises from the ashes] After Turnus falls, Ardea is burned by ruthless flames and its houses collapse into hot embers. A bird rises from the ruins and mourns the city with its wings.

l: deification of Aeneas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus asks Jupiter to grant Aeneas godhead after his heroic deeds, and Jupiter assents with Juno’s approval. Numicius washes away Aeneas’s mortality, Venus anoints him with divine substances, and he becomes a god called Indiges.

l: birds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: resemble swans [though not actually swans] Venus transforms Diomedes’s companions into birds resembling white swans, and the transformed birds fly around the oars. Another bird emerges from the burning ruins of Ardea and retains the city’s name and signs of mourning.

l: ships of Aeneas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: are_transformed_into sea nymphs [by Cybele] Turnus sets fire to Aeneas’s ships, but Cybele saves them from destruction. She transforms the ships into sea Nymphs with flesh, fingers, swimming feet, hair, and arms.

l: Pomona, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pomona is a Nymph and Hamadryad of Latium, the finest tender of gardens, devoted to fruit trees, country, pruning, grafting, and watering roots. She initially rejects love, marriage, and male approach, enclosing her orchard and fearing rustics. Under Proca, she has a priest called Flamen Pomonalis. After hearing Vertumnus’s account of Anaxarete, she is captivated by his youthful form and returns his love.

l: Vertumnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Vertumnus is a shape-shifting god, a tutelary deity of traders at Rome, associated with seasonal change and said by some to have been an ancient king of Etruria. He has a temple in Vicus Tuscus. Loving Pomona above all other suitors and sharing her tastes for fruit and gardens, he repeatedly disguises himself to reach her, speaks as an old woman, tells of Anaxarete and Iphis, then returns to youthful form.

l: Romans, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romans are a group descended from Æneas. Protected by Venus and the Naiads during the Sabine attack, they fight under Romulus and then share peace, laws, and sovereignty with the Sabines. They invite Numa to receive sovereignty, credit his peaceful legal reforms to Egeria, and seek her after her transformation. They later heed Cippus’s warning, mourn his exile, and honor him with a statue.

l: marriage, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Marriage is presented to Pomona through the example of an elm and vine joined together, each benefiting from the other. The disguised Vertumnus urges her to abandon her avoidance of marriage and choose Vertumnus as the partner of her couch.

l: disguises of Vertumnus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: symbolize change of seasons [possibly through spring, harvest, and winter] Vertumnus takes the forms of a reaper, a haymaker, an ox-driver, a woodman, a pruner of vines, a fruit-gatherer, a soldier, and a fisherman to gain access to Pomona. He later assumes the shape of an old woman, wearing a coloured cap and leaning on a stick, and uses that disguise to advise her to marry him.

l: Anaxarete, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Anaxarete, a noblewoman descended from Teucer, cruelly rejects Iphis’s repeated appeals. After witnessing his funeral procession, she is fixed in place and transformed into stone; Salamis preserves her statue beneath a temple called Venus, the looker-out.

l: Iphis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Iphis is a humble-born man whose unrequited love for Anaxarete drives repeated pleas through her household, letters, and garlands; rejected, he hangs himself before her door, and his body is taken for burial.

l: Amulius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Amulius, a wicked ruler of Ausonia, dies before Numitor regains the kingdom with his grandsons’ aid.

l: Numitor, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a aged king [the rightful ruler restored with the aid of his grandsons] Numitor regains the kingdom that he had lost after the death of Amulius, aided by his grandsons.

l: Romulus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus is Rome’s founder, first king, lawgiver, and ruler of the Romans. Married to Hersilia, he leads Rome’s war against Tatius and the Sabines, then shares sovereignty with Tatius. His spear, thrown from Mount Aventine toward the Capitol, takes root and becomes a tree presaging Rome’s greatness. Finally Gradivus takes him from earth to heaven, and he is deified as Quirinus.

l: Tatius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tatius, a Sabine king, wages war against Romulus with the Sabine fathers; after losses bring peace, he shares sovereignty with Romulus until his death.

l: the Sabines, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Sabines, from Cures, wage war on the Romans under Tatius, enter Rome through an opened gate, are stopped and fight, then join Romans in shared peace and government.

l: Tarpeia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_killed_by the Sabines [after opening the gate to them for their ornaments] Tarpeia loses her life after the way to the citadel is opened. The Sabines heap their arms upon her, killing her.

l: the Naiads of Ausonia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Naiads of Ausonia are nymphs associated with Janus’s fountain; answering Venus, they heat its springs with sulphur, fire, and pitch, blocking the Sabines and protecting the Romans.

l: Mavors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Mavors, a poetic name of Mars, asks the father of Gods and men to raise Romulus and his established Roman state to heaven.

l: Hersilia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hersilia, Romulus’s wife, mourns him, ascends to heaven by a falling star, reunites with him, and is deified as Ora.

l: Ora, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a goddess [deified form of Hersilia] Ora is the new name given to Hersilia when Romulus receives her in heaven. She remains united with Quirinus.

l: Palatium, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a hill [wooded hill where Romulus is taken to heaven] The hill of the woody Palatium is where Gradivus lands after descending through the air and takes Romulus from the earth.

l: the Roman-Sabine war, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: ends_in peace [with shared sovereignty] The Roman-Sabine war begins when Tatius and the Sabine fathers attack Rome after entering through an opened gate. It ends when Roman and Sabine blood has been shed and the two sides agree to peace, shared sovereignty, and common laws.

l: the founding of Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a founding of a city [associated with Romulus and the festival of Pales] The walls of Rome are founded on the festival of Pales after Numitor regains his kingdom. Romulus is identified as the founder of the city and its first king.

l: Iphis's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: causes Anaxarete's transformation into stone [after Anaxarete witnesses his funeral] Iphis's suicide occurs before Anaxarete's door after her prolonged rejection has made his love unbearable. He fastens a halter to the door, places his head in the noose, and hangs himself while turned toward her.

l: Anaxarete's transformation into stone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a mythic transformation [explained as a metaphor for extreme insensibility] Anaxarete's transformation occurs when she looks from an upper room at Iphis's funeral procession. Her eyes and body stiffen, and the stone already present in her cruel breast takes possession of her limbs.

l: Romulus's apotheosis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a deification [Romulus is taken to heaven] Romulus's apotheosis is requested by Mavors and approved by the all-powerful God after Rome has become firmly established. Gradivus carries Romulus from the Palatium to heaven, where he assumes the divine form and name of Quirinus.

l: Hersilia's apotheosis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a deification [Hersilia ascends to heaven and is received by Romulus] Hersilia's apotheosis follows Iris's guidance to the hill of Romulus. A falling star sets her hair ablaze and carries her to heaven, where Romulus receives her and changes her name to Ora.

l: the fountain of Janus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The fountain of Janus near the Naiads of Ausonia is heated with sulphur, fire, and pitch, becoming an impassable fiery barrier to the Sabines.

l: the gates of Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The gates of Rome are opened by Juno to admit the Sabines, but a heated fountain near Janus blocks the approach until the Romans are ready to fight.

l: the Roman constitution and kingship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_established strong foundation [after Rome is no longer dependent on one guardian] Romulus initially rules Rome as its king. After the Roman-Sabine conflict, Romulus and Tatius give laws in common to both peoples and share sovereignty, while Romulus's later apotheosis establishes him as Quirinus.

l: Myscelos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos, an Argive son of Alemon favoured by the Gods, is commanded by Hercules in a dream to leave Argos for land by the Æsar. Though tried under Argive law forbidding departure, Hercules aids his acquittal; he sails to Italy and founds Crotona.

l: Crotona, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Crotona is a place in Italy, founded by Myscelos during Numa Pompilius’s fourth year near Æsar’s destined mouth, and named for Croton, whose sacred bones lie beneath a mound.

l: Æsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a river [in Calabria] The Æsar is a distant river in Italy whose pebbly streams Hercules commands Myscelos to seek. Myscelos eventually finds its destined mouth near the site where he establishes Crotona.

l: Myscelos's dream, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: In the dream, Hercules twice commands Myscelos to leave his native abodes and repair to the Æsar. The second appearance includes more numerous and severe threats if Myscelos disobeys.

l: Myscelos's trial, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Myscelos is accused of holding the laws of Argos in contempt when he prepares to depart. Although every pebble initially cast into the urn is black, Hercules changes them all to white, and Myscelos is acquitted.

l: founding of Crotona, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: After reaching Italy, Myscelos finds the place where Croton's sacred bones are buried and builds walls on the appointed land. He transfers Croton's name to the city, establishing Crotona on the Italian coast.

l: Pythagoras, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras is a Samian-born philosopher who voluntarily leaves Samos through hatred of tyranny, travels through Asia, and settles at Crotona in Italy. After studying the nature of things, he publicly teaches and promulgates Pythagorean philosophy, investigating the universe’s origin and nature and teaching gods, natural phenomena, the soul, abstinence from animal food, and continual change. He holds that nothing perishes, identifies himself with Euphorbus in a former incarnation, forbids animal sacrifice for food, and advocates vegetarianism because souls may inhabit animals and flesh pollutes bodies. His reputation is said to draw Numa Pompilius, though this timing is disputed; Livy places him under Servius Tullius.

l: Pythagorean philosophy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagorean philosophy centers on metempsychosis and transformation: souls are not destroyed but continually pass into new bodies, while physical forms change without permanent destruction. Presented through Pythagoras, it connects these teachings to abstinence from animal food and the principle that nothing in the universe remains permanently one form.

l: the origin and nature of the universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pythagoras investigates and explains the origin of the vast universe, the causes of things, the meaning of nature, and the nature of God. He also considers snow, lightning, earthquakes, and the courses of the stars.

l: animal sacrifice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_attributed_to the Gods [wrongly, according to Pythagoras] Animal sacrifice is condemned as a wickedness that humans have wrongly attributed to the gods. Animals are decorated, placed on altars, killed, and then examined through their entrails for divine intentions.

l: vegetarianism, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_available_from the earth [without slaughter and bloodshed] Pythagoras is described as the first to forbid animals from being served at table. He recommends corn, apples, grapes, herbs, milk, and honey instead of flesh, arguing that the earth supplies agreeable food without slaughter or bloodshed.

l: the transmigration of souls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a continuing passage of souls between bodies [including animals and humans] The transmigration of souls teaches that a soul leaves one body and inhabits another, passing between human and animal bodies. Pythagoras claims that he himself was once Euphorbus and later recognized Euphorbus's shield in a temple at Argos.

l: the soul, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The soul is immortal, not subject to death; leaving one dwelling, it remains the same while living on in different bodies and forms.

l: Time, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a constant progression [likened to a flowing river] Time moves continually and cannot stop, like a river. Earlier moments pass away, moments that did not exist come into being, and each minute is replaced by another.

l: change and transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Change and transformation are continual and universal in the physical world. Across time, heavens, seasons, bodies, landscapes, waters, cities, nations, and souls, nothing wholly perishes: forms cease to be what they were and assume new appearances, from tadpoles and coral to fallen cities and migrating souls.

l: the four elements, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The four elements are everlasting elementary bodies: earth and water, heavy, move downward; air and fire, light, seek higher regions.

l: water, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a heavy element [borne downward by its weight] Water is one of the heavy elements and can evaporate into air or become dense and form earth. Particular waters are described as freezing, warming, becoming bitter, changing bodies or minds, or disappearing and reappearing in new channels.

l: air, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a light element [seeking the higher regions] Air is a light element that seeks the higher regions. As water evaporates, it becomes air, and as fire becomes gross, it passes into dense air.

l: fire, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a light element [purer than air and seeking the higher regions] Fire is lighter than air and seeks the highest regions. It can become dense air, and volcanic fire may arise from winds, rocky friction, bituminous matter, or sulphur; when its fuel is exhausted, it will eventually die.

l: the universe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The universe, everlasting and containing four elementary bodies, preserves all things as forms vary and parts move, with nothing perishing.

l: Trœzen, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Trœzen honored Hippolytus after his death by building him a temple and appointing a priest to offer annual sacrifices. Its young women were said to cut off their hair before marriage and carry it to his temple.

l: animals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Animals include grass-fed horses, sheep, and herds, and blood-feeding tigers, lions, bears, and wolves. They may suffer human slaughter, serve humans in life, receive transmigrating souls, and be used for sacrifice despite prohibition.

l: the elements' cycle of transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: transforms the four elements [in a recurring cycle] The elements pass through a recurring cycle: earth dissolves into water, water evaporates into air, air rises into fire, fire becomes dense air, air becomes water, and dense water forms earth. No element retains its own form permanently, because nature continually reshapes one into another.

l: metempsychosis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Metempsychosis is a doctrine of continual soul transmigration, transferring human souls between bodies; it leads people to protect animals because they may contain souls of parents, brothers, allies, or other humans.

l: vegetarian abstinence, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_practiced_by Pythagorean philosophy [because souls may inhabit animals] there are persons,] Vegetarian abstinence is urged because animals may contain the souls of human relatives or other people. The speaker condemns killing calves, kids, and birds for food and recommends that animals be used for plowing, wool, or milk instead, while people consume more suitable sustenance.

l: human souls, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: enter animals [as their abode through transmigration] there are persons,] Human souls are described as fleeting portions of the universe that can enter the bodies of animals and hide within cattle. Because of this possibility, the speaker says that bodies containing the souls of parents, brothers, allies, or other people should remain safe and unharmed.

l: Nymph Egeria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Egeria is a nymph and Numa’s wife, associated with advising him on laws. After Numa’s death, she withdraws to Aricia’s groves and grieves so deeply that she disrupts Diana’s rites. Unconsoled, she is transformed by Diana into a cool, ever-flowing fountain in her grove.

l: Hippolytus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus, son of Theseus and, in differing accounts, Hippolyta or Antiope, was raised at Trœzen by Pittheus. Described as wise, chaste, and hostile to voluptuousness, he pursued hunting and chariot racing. His rejection of Phædra led to her false accusation that he sought to defile his father’s couch; Theseus exiled and cursed him. On the road toward Trœzen, a sea-monster frightened his horses, overturning his chariot and killing him. He received divine honors, was restored through Apollo’s son’s remedies, transformed and known in Italy as Virbius, and was also said to be translated to heaven as Auriga.

l: Virbius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Virbius, Diana’s devoted lower God, is Hippolytus renamed after restoration to life and lives concealed under her protection in her grove.

l: Tages, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages is a diviner and first teacher of Etruscan divination. He arose from a fate-revealing clod moving in a field, took human form, announced future destinies, and taught the Etrurian nation to foretell events; his unknown origin led to his being called son of the earth.

l: Genucius Cippus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Genucius Cippus is a Roman figure associated with a prodigy: horn-like growths, or horns, appeared on his forehead after he returned victorious from conquest. An Etrurian soothsayer or augurs interpreted the omen to mean that, if he entered or reentered Rome, he would become king. Rejecting kingship and fearing Rome’s loss of liberty, he summoned the people and Senate and chose voluntary exile or banishment. Rome rewarded his patriotism with land, said to be as much as he could encircle with yoked oxen in a day, and with a brazen statue. In Ovid’s version, he returns after assisting Consul Valerius.

l: sea-monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The sea-monster appears when the sea rises like a mountain and divides, sending forth a horned bull that vomits seawater. Its appearance terrifies Hippolytus's horses and causes them to drive his chariot over the rocks.

l: Hippolytus's chariot, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_broken_by stump [at the wheel and long axle-tree] Hippolytus's chariot was driven toward the lofty rocks when his horses panicked at the sea-monster. Its wheel struck a stump and broke apart on the long axle-tree, throwing Hippolytus out and leaving the reins entangled around his limbs.

l: Romulus's lance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus's lance, fixed in the Palatine hill, formed roots, became a cornel-tree with flexible twigs, shaded astonished spectators, and was interpreted as a presage of Rome's future greatness.

l: fountain of Egeria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a cool fountain [formed from Egeria's body] The fountain of Egeria was formed when Diana transformed Egeria's grieving body and dissolved her limbs into ever-flowing waters.

l: Cippus's horns, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cippus’s horns appeared on his forehead, were confirmed in water, foretold kingship if he entered the city, and were later carved on Rome’s brass-decorated doorposts.

l: death of Numa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa dies after a long reign and life; Romans, Latian matrons, Senators, and Egeria mourn him.

l: death of Hippolytus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_caused_by sea-monster [the monster frightens his horses] Hippolytus died after his father's curse and exile led him toward Trœzen. A sea-monster frightened his horses, his chariot broke against a stump, and his body was dragged and torn apart by the reins and surrounding obstacles.

l: resurrection of Hippolytus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippolytus, opposed by Pluto, is restored to life by Apollo's son's remedies, potent herbs, and Pæonian aid; Diana conceals, transforms, and renames him Virbius.

l: transformation of Egeria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Egeria's overwhelming grief caused her to fall at the base of a hill and dissolve into tears. Moved by her affection, Diana transformed her body into a cool fountain whose waters flowed continually.

l: appearance of Tages, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Tages appeared when a clod of earth moved without being touched, assumed human form, and lost its earthly shape. His newly formed mouth delivered the decrees of future destiny.

l: transformation of Romulus's lance, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Romulus's lance changed from an iron-pointed dart into a rooted tree. It grew limber twigs and provided an unexpected shade on the Palatine hill.

l: Cippus's voluntary exile, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: preserves liberty of Rome [by refusing kingship] Cippus voluntarily chose exile after learning that entering the city would make him king. He declared that he would rather live in exile than allow the Capitol to see him as king, and the nobles granted him as much land as he could enclose with a plough in one day.

l: kingship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Numa received kingship after the Roman people voluntarily invited him to rule. Cippus was told that he would become king if he entered the city, but he rejected the offered kingship because it would threaten the people's freedom.

l: liberty of Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cippus acts to preserve Rome's liberty by refusing to enter the city as the prophesied king. He warns the Romans that his entry would subject them to his laws as slaves and urges them to exclude or bind him.

l: divination, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: spreads_from ancient Etrurians [over the whole of Italy] Divination by means of water, called Hydromancy, was associated with the fountain in the Arician grove and was said to have been used by Numa. The ancient Etrurians practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of beasts and observing the flight of birds, and this system spread throughout Italy.

l: Arician grove, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: The Arician grove was the place where Numa was said to retire in order to consult the Nymph Egeria. The Romans later searched the grove for Egeria and found only a fountain at the spot Numa had frequented.

l: Phædra, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Phædra is sent to Athens by Deucalion, falls in love with Hippolytus, and builds the Hippolyteum near Trœzen to see him. After his rejection, she accuses him in a letter to Theseus and dies by suicide, though one account places her death after learning of his death.

l: Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius, son of Apollo and Coronis, is a god of saving and health-restoring who protects Epidaurus. Sought by Romans during pestilence, he promises aid in a dream, travels as a serpent to Rome, and ends the disease on the Island of the Tiber.

l: pestilence, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: A contagion ravages Rome, wasting bodies despite mortal efforts and medical skill, until Æsculapius comes and it ends.

l: disease, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: dries_up blood [through consumption] Disease afflicts Rome so severely that the people seek help from heaven after physicians prove ineffective. Æsculapius is brought to the city to put an end to it.

l: Epidaurus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a city [inhabited by Æsculapius] Epidaurus is the city where the youthful son of Phoebus, Æsculapius, dwells. Its people debate whether to surrender their guardian deity, but Æsculapius chooses to leave and travel with the Romans.

l: serpent, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: A golden, fiery-eyed serpent, a form of Æsculapius and recognized as God, travels by Roman ship to Rome, leaves at the Island of the Tiber, and resumes celestial form.

l: Æsculapius cult, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Æsculapius cult enters Rome after a serpent reaches the Island of the Tiber, becoming a refuge for disease, especially pestilence.

l: Island of the Tiber, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: An island within the Tiber at Rome, formed by two equal river channels, becomes Æsculapius’s chosen habitation, introducing his cult and ending the city’s mourning.

l: Tiber Island temple, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_built_on Island of the Tiber [for Æsculapius] A temple is built on the Island of the Tiber in honor of Æsculapius after the serpent chooses the site. The temple serves as the Roman place associated with the god’s healing presence.

l: serpent voyage to Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: transports Æsculapius [from Epidaurus to Rome] The serpent travels from Epidaurus aboard an Ausonian ship, passing along the Italian coast and through the Sicilian straits before reaching the mouths of the Tiber. At Rome, it leaves the ship and settles on the Island of the Tiber.

l: Temple of Æsculapius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_built_for Æsculapius [on the Island of the Tiber] A temple is built in honor of Æsculapius after his arrival in Rome and the cessation of the pestilence. The explanation identifies the temple as being on the Island of the Tiber.

l: conspirators, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Conspirators treacherously carry drawn swords into the Senate-house, brandish them against Julius Cæsar, and murder him despite the Gods' warnings.

l: Senate-house, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_the_site_of assassination of Julius Cæsar The Senate-house is selected by the conspirators as the place for Julius Cæsar’s crime and murder. Venus enters it invisibly after the assassination to rescue his soul from his body.

l: star of Julius Cæsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_the_abode_of Julius Cæsar [after his apotheosis] The star of Julius Cæsar is formed when Venus carries his soul upward and drops it from her bosom. It shines above the moon with a long, flaming train and looks down upon the Capitol and Forum.

l: Julius Cæsar’s apotheosis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_a deification [represented as transformation into a star] Julius Cæsar’s apotheosis occurs when his soul is transformed into a beam of light and established among the stars. The transformation fulfills Venus’s desire that he be made divine rather than remain sprung only from mortal seed.

l: assassination of Julius Cæsar, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: occurs_in Senate-house [through conspiratorial treachery] The assassination of Julius Cæsar is foretold by ominous signs, including strange sounds in the heavens, bloodlike rain, weeping statues, unfavorable entrails, ghosts, and earthquakes. The warnings cannot prevent the conspirators from murdering him in the Senate-house.

l: Augustus’s reign, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: includes Roman law and civil rights [after peace is granted to the earth] Augustus’s reign is described as extending over the habitable world and the sea. After granting peace to the earth, he is expected to turn to civil rights, enact laws, regulate manners, and continue his rule into old age.

l: Ovid’s immortality through poetry, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: is_achieved_through The Metamorphoses [by being read throughout the ages] The Poet claims that his work will survive anger, fire, steel, and consuming time. Although his body will eventually die, his better part and indelible name will live wherever Roman power extends and throughout all ages.

l: The Library
s: This is Volume II of Apollodorus’s The Library in the Loeb Classical Library, translated into English by Sir James George Frazer. It contains the continuation of Book III, the Epitome, an appendix, notes, and an index. Its main mythological narrative moves through divine and heroic genealogies into the histories of Troy, Athens, the Trojan War, and its aftermath. It begins with Atlas and Pleione’s Pleiades and follows lines of descent including Hermes, Aesculapius, the Dioscuri, Dardanus, Priam, Paris, Achilles, and the Trojan royal house. It recounts foundations, sacred objects, prophecies, abductions, crimes, transformations, and successions, notably the Palladium’s arrival at Ilium, Paris’s survival and later abduction of Helen, and Achilles’s upbringing and departure for Troy. A major central sequence concerns Athens: Cecrops, Athena’s victory over Poseidon for Attica, the kings Cranaus, Erichthonius, Pandion, and Erechtheus, and tragedies involving Procne, Philomela, and Tereus. It then follows Aegeus and Theseus: the Minotaur tribute and labyrinth, Theseus’s clearing of the road to Athens, his killing of the Minotaur with Ariadne’s help, Aegeus’s death, Daedalus and Icarus’s escape, and Theseus’s later downfall after the Dioscuri recover Helen. The Epitome develops the Pelopid conflict of Atreus and Thyestes, then the expedition against Troy prompted by Helen’s abduction. It traces the Greeks’ preparations, Iphigenia’s rescue by Artemis, the siege, Patroclus’s death, Achilles’s killing of Hector and later death, the recovery of Philoctetes and Neoptolemus, theft of the Palladium, and the Wooden Horse. Troy is sacked, followed by disastrous Greek returns, Agamemnon’s murder and Orestes’s revenge, Menelaus’s restoration, and Odysseus’s wanderings, homecoming, and death at Telegonus’s hands. The appendix compares selected Greek tales with accounts from many other peoples: fire and renewal, magical revivification, Oedipus-like incest stories, twins and fertility, Peleus and Thetis as a supernatural-spouse tale, Idomeneus’s vow, and especially widespread variants of the Ulysses and Polyphemus story. Notes and the extensive alphabetical index provide genealogical, textual, and mythological reference material.

l: Loeb Classical Library, The Library
s: Loeb Classical Library, edited by E. Capps, T. E. Page, and W. H. D. Rouse, published Apollodorus's The Library in Volume II.

l: Apollodorus, The Library
s: Apollodorus is the author of The Library and a source for several mythic accounts. His record of Troy includes its sack, Astyanax’s killing, Polyxena’s sacrifice, and the division of captive women among Greek leaders. In the account of the child on the fire, he names Celeus and Metanira as Demophon’s parents, distinguishes Demophon from Triptolemus, and says Praxithea’s interruption led to the child’s being consumed. He tells of Melampus and kine held by Phylacus, and reports that Leucus’s crimes and alliance led to Idomeneus’s expulsion. He also gives the Pleiades’ names in Aratus’s order.

l: The Library, The Library
s: The Library, a two-volume work by Apollodorus, appears in a 1921 English translation by Sir James George Frazer; Volume II continues Book III and adds Epitome, Appendix, Index.

l: Sir James George Frazer, The Library
s: is_a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge Sir James George Frazer provided the English translation of The Library. He is identified as a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and is listed with the designations F.B.A. and F.R.S.

l: Ἴλτλαντος, The Library
s: is_parent_of θυγατέρες ἑπτὰ Ἴλτλαντος was the father of seven daughters born in Κυλλήνῃ of ᾿Αρκαδίας.

l: ᾿Ωκεανοῦ Πλειόνη, The Library
s: is_parent_of θυγατέρες ἑπτὰ ᾿Ωκεανοῦ Πλειόνη was the mother of seven daughters born in Κυλλήνῃ of ᾿Αρκαδίας.

l: θυγατέρες ἑπτὰ, The Library
s: Seven daughters, born to Ἴλτλαντος and ᾿Ωκεανοῦ Πλειόνη, are located in Κυλλήνῃ of ᾿Αρκαδίας.

l: αἱ Ἰ]ληιάδες, The Library
s: αἱ Ἰ]ληιάδες are seven daughters, including ᾿Αλκυόνη, Μερόπη, Κελαινὼ, λέκτρα, Στερόπη, and Ταῦγέτη.

l: Pleiades, The Library
s: Pleiades are a group of seven daughters, generally identified as Alcyone, Merope, Celaeno, Electra, Sterope, Taygete, and Maia. They were born at Cyllene in Arcadia and are described as daughters of Atlas and Pleione; Atlas was commonly said to be their father, giving them the name Atlantides. One account instead makes them daughters of the queen of the Amazons, and the origin of the name Pleiades was disputed among the ancients. Their names were generally agreed upon, though the Scholiast on Theocritus offered a different list except for Maia. They are discussed across numerous works, from Phaenomena and Catasterismi to Astronomica, Fasti, and later commentaries.

l: Maia, The Library
s: Maia, eldest daughter of Atlas and Pleione, bears Hermes by Zeus in a cave of Cyllene.

l: Amazons, The Library
s: The Amazons, companions of Hippolyte, fought with Hercules against Theseus, who carried off Antiope or Melanippe. They later marched on Athens and were defeated. At Phaedra’s wedding, they appeared armed and threatened the guests; battle followed, killing Hippolyte and, in another account, an Amazon previously married to Theseus.

l: Atlas, The Library
s: is_parent_of Pleiades [father] Atlas had seven daughters by Pleione, who were called the Pleiades.

l: origin of the name Pleiades, The Library
s: is_derived_from mother (the Pleiades' mother) [according to some accounts] The origin of the name Pleiades was the subject of diverse opinions among ancient writers. The text begins to report that some derived the name from the name of their mother, but does not provide further details.

l: Pleione, The Library
s: Ocean’s daughter Pleione, mother with Atlas of seven daughters called the Pleiades.

l: Alcyone, The Library
s: is_parent_of Aethusa [daughter] Poseidon had intercourse with Alcyone, and she bore Aethusa, Hyrieus, and Hyperenor.

l: Merope, The Library
s: Merope was married to Sisyphus.

l: Celaeno, The Library
s: Poseidon had intercourse with Celaeno, and she bore Lycus, whom Poseidon made to dwell in the Islands of the Blest.

l: Electra, The Library
s: Electra appears as daughter of Atlas, who bears Iasion and Dardanus by Zeus, and as daughter of Agamemnon, who saves Orestes, entrusts him to Strophius, and is later married by Orestes to Pylades.

l: Oenomaus, The Library
s: Oenomaus, king of Pisa and father of Hippodamia, possessed arms and horses given by Ares. He made her marriage a contest, pursued suitors in armor, killed those he overtook, and displayed their heads. He was eventually killed or died after losing the race to Pelops.

l: Poseidon, The Library
s: Poseidon is a deity closely associated with the sea, divine transformations, parentage, gifts, vengeance, and acts of destruction. He fathers many figures in differing accounts, including Lycus by Celaeno, Aethusa, Hyrieus, and Hyperenor by Alcyone, Triton by Amphitrite, Polyphemus by Thoösa, Neleus, Nauplius, Thasus in one tradition, and others; he also has unions with Aethra and is named in genealogies involving Asopus, Cychreus, Rhode, Salamis, Sarpedon, and Scamander’s lineage. He makes Lycus dwell in the Islands of the Blest. He first arrives in Attica, strikes the Acropolis with his trident to produce the sea Erechtheis, and contests Athena for Attica. After the twelve gods favor Athena, he floods the Thriasian plain in anger. Later, after Eumolpus is killed, he destroys Erechtheus and his house. He favors Pelops, his beloved and minion, giving him a winged chariot that can run through the sea without wet axles; he also receives Pelops’ prayer. He gives Xanthus to Peleus, receives the dedication of Argo, fortifies Pergamum with Apollo, and is connected with Minos’s unkept vow to sacrifice a bull. He answers Theseus’s prayer against Hippolytus by sending a bull from the surf, which terrifies the horses and wrecks the chariot. After Polyphemus is blinded, Poseidon is wrathful toward Odysseus and angry with the Phaeacians for aiding him: he breaks Odysseus’s raft, petrifies their ship, and encloses their city with a mountain. Odysseus later propitiates him among the Thesprotians.

l: Apollo, The Library
s: Apollo is a deity whose records center on cattle-herding, exchange, prophecy, kinship, punishment, and deadly power. While herding cattle, he pursued Hermes for stealing them, searched at Pylus, accused him before Maia, brought him to Zeus, and ultimately gave the cattle in exchange for the lyre; he also gave Hermes a golden wand. He loved Coronis, fathered Aesculapius with her in one genealogy, killed Coronis after she chose Ischys, rescued Aesculapius from her pyre, then killed the Cyclopes in anger over Aesculapius’s death. By Zeus’s command he served Admetus for a year as a herdsman, tending unusually fertile animals said to bear twins. He killed Python, cursed Raven, and, with Artemis, killed Niobe’s children. He promised Cassandra prophecy for her favours, granted the art, and after her refusal deprived it of persuasive power. He is also said to father Troilus, Miletus, and Mopsus; to send serpents as a sign to the Trojans; to reconcile Odysseus with Athena; and to be fated to kill Achilles if Achilles kills Tenes. Later accounts connect him with the plundering and burning of his temple at Delphi by Neoptolemus.

l: Antiope, The Library
s: Antiope, an Amazon, was carried off by Theseus, married him, and became mother of Zethus and Amphion by Zeus.

l: Zeus, The Library
s: Zeus is a god, son of Cronus and Rhea, born in a cave of Dicte in Crete, fed by nymphs and guarded by Curetes. After making war on the Titans and shutting them in Tartarus, he receives dominion over the sky by lot. He becomes Hera’s husband, though their relationship includes his fear of her and his binding and hanging her from Olympus. He possesses the aegis, ordains oaths by Styx, appoints gods and Hermes to duties, judges disputes, and repeatedly directs divine and mortal affairs. His rule is marked by conflict and punishment: he fights Typhon and giants, casts Etna on Typhon, and uses thunderbolts against Aesculapius, Idas, Iasion, Salmoneus, Capaneus, and others. He binds Ixion, orders Prometheus nailed to the Caucasus, causes a flood to destroy the men of the Bronze Age, transforms or punishes figures such as Io, Ceyx, Alcyone, and Lycaon, and strikes Ulysses’s ship after the slaughter of the Sun’s cattle. He also aids or orders Hermes in many missions, appoints Aeolus keeper of the winds, and determines outcomes involving Adonis, Atreus, Alexander, and Attica. Zeus has numerous unions, often through disguises or abduction, and fathers many gods, heroes, and rulers. His children include Hermes, the Muses, Helen, Pollux, Castor, Aeacus, Iasion, Dardanus, Dionysus, Perseus, Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, Amphion, Zethus, Pan, Hellen, and Lacedaemon. He carries Europa to Crete as a bull, approaches Leda and Nemesis as a swan, impregnates Danae as a stream of gold, and takes Aegina away. The records conclude by emphasizing his broad intervention in the affairs of gods, heroes, cities, births, punishments, and major events.

l: Hermes, The Library
s: Hermes is the son of Zeus and Maia, born in a cave of Cyllene, and a herald to Zeus, the infernal gods, and the gods generally. Early, he steals Apollo’s cattle, sacrifices some, makes a lyre, exchanges it for the cattle, and gains Apollo’s golden wand, divination, and appointment as herald. He makes a shepherd’s pipe, fathers Cephalus and Abderus, carries messages and gives or guides others with important objects. His deeds include killing Hippolytus and Argus, rescuing Ares, aiding Perseus, Hercules, and Ulysses, bringing up Protesilaus from Hades, and giving Helen to Proteus for protection.

l: Cyllene, The Library
s: Cyllene was the place where the Pleiades were born and where Maia gave birth to Hermes in a cave. Hermes returned there after stealing Apollo's cattle, and Apollo went there to accuse him.

l: Pylus, The Library
s: Pylus is a place where Hermes brings Apollo’s cattle and hides the rest; Apollo searches, questions its inhabitants, and receives them there, before Melampus brings kine and gives them to Neleus as a bridal gift.

l: cave of Cyllene, The Library
s: The cave of Cyllene was where Maia gave birth to Hermes. Hermes was shown there by Maia after Apollo accused him.

l: theoi, The Library
s: The gods pity Smyrna after she prays to become invisible and transform her into the tree called smyrna, or myrrh.

l: cattle, The Library
s: The cattle were being herded by Apollo when Hermes stole them and took them to Pylus. Hermes hid some, sacrificed two, and later returned the cattle to Apollo in exchange for the lyre. Apollo was said to have increased the fertility of Admetus's cattle by causing all the cows to bear twins. In Nandi belief, a mother of twins approaching cattle could cause the animals to die.

l: tortoise, The Library
s: Hermes found a tortoise browsing before the cave at Cyllene. He cleaned out its shell and used it to make a lyre.

l: lyre, The Library
s: Hermes made the lyre from a tortoise shell and cords made from the cattle he had sacrificed. Apollo exchanged the cattle for the lyre after hearing it.

l: golden wand, The Library
s: Apollo offered Hermes the golden wand that he had possessed while herding cattle in exchange for Hermes's shepherd's pipe. Hermes also sought the art of divination.

l: shepherd's pipe, The Library
s: While herding the cattle, Hermes made a shepherd's pipe and played it. Apollo wanted it and offered his golden wand in exchange.

l: cattle theft by Hermes, The Library
s: Hermes stole the cattle that Apollo was herding, taking them to Pylus and attempting to conceal the tracks. Apollo discovered through divination who had stolen them and accused Hermes.

l: exchange of the lyre for the cattle, The Library
s: After Hermes returned the cattle to Pylus, Apollo heard the lyre and gave the cattle to Hermes in exchange for it.

l: Hermes's appointment as herald, The Library
s: Zeus appointed Hermes as herald to himself and to the infernal gods.

l: Tyndareus, The Library
s: Tyndareus, said to be son of Oebalus and Batia, was expelled from Lacedaemon by Hippocoon and his sons. After their deaths, he returned and ruled, married Leda, fathered Clytaemnestra, brought back Agamemnon and Menelaus, chose Menelaus for Helen, bound her suitors by oath, and gave Menelaus Sparta’s kingdom.

l: Icarius, The Library
s: Icarius, a father of Penelope and husband of Periboea, is exiled from Lacedaemon with Tyndareus by Hippocoon and his sons, then returns after Heracles kills them. Dionysus teaches him wine-making; shepherds kill him after undiluted wine makes them think they are bewitched, and Maera helps Erigone find his body.

l: Lynceus, The Library
s: Lynceus, son of Aphareus, has exceptional sight, even underground. While driving Arcadian cattle booty with Idas, Castor, and Pollux, he finds Castor and tells Idas, who kills him; Lynceus wounds Pollux before Pollux kills him with a spear.

l: Idas, The Library
s: Idas, called a son of Aphareus and in many accounts a child of Poseidon, divides cattle booty by a trick, eating his and Lynceus’s shares to claim the cattle. He drives them to Messene, kills Castor after Lynceus reveals him, wounds Pollux, and is killed by Zeus’s thunderbolt.

l: Dioscuri, The Library
s: Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, a pair of twin heroic gods named for their bravery and manliness: Castor practiced warfare and Pollux boxing. They fought in Messene over cattle booty and other spoil, carried off and married Hilaira and Phoebe, captured Athens with the Lacedaemonians and Arcadians, carried away Helen and Aethra, and restored Menestheus to sovereignty. After Castor’s death, Zeus granted the pair alternating existence among gods and mortals.

l: Aesculapius, The Library
s: Aesculapius, alternatively said to be Arsinoe’s son, was brought from Coronis’s pyre to Chiron, who taught him healing and hunting. Becoming a skilled surgeon, he prevented deaths and used Gorgon’s blood received from Athena to raise Tyndareus, Glaucus, Pelops, and others.
